ety.text: From Middle English haha, ha ha, from Old English ha ha (interjection), ultimately onomatopoeic. Compare Old Frisian haha (interjection), Middle Low German hahā, hahahā (interjection), Middle High German hahā, haha (interjection), all expressions of joy or of laughter.

Borrowed from French haha. The French term attested 1686 in toponyms in New France (present-day Quebec); compare modern Saint-Louis-du-Ha! Ha!. Usual etymology is that an expression of surprise – “ha ha” or “ah! ah!” is exclaimed on encountering such a boundary. In France this is traditionally attributed to the reaction of Louis, Grand Dauphin to encountering such a feature in the gardens of the Château de Meudon.

ex: Emett yelled for him, and Jones and Jim “hahaed!”
She haha’d like she ate diamonds for breakfast and flossed with spun gold.

senses.d: A type of boundary to a garden, pleasure-ground, or park, designed not to interrupt the view and to be invisible until closely approached.
A large leafy Hawaiian plant, Gunnera petaloidea.

ety.text: Onomatopoeic. In Spanish, "j" is pronounced as /x/, akin to /h/, the natural sound of human laughter.
Hawaiian hāhābor. English hahaubor. Portuguese haha Unadapted borrowing from English haha.

From quá-quá-quá or quiá-quiá-quiá, of onomatopoeic origin. Attested since at least 2002. The laugh originated among Brazilians, but today is also used by the Portuguese and other Portuguese speakers. Compare Korean ㅋ (k), which gave origin to English kek.
